For 2025 to 2026 Lynchburg taxes real estate at $0.84 per $100 of total assessed value. City Council sets that figure, so confirm it for the year you are selling. The City Assessor page carries the details, and a ParcelViewer map tool there shows property records.

The office is open Monday through Friday, 8:30 am to 5 pm.

Two city offices split the work. The Assessor puts values on parcels, and the Treasurer sends bills and takes payment. The Assessor's office works under Chapter 18-48 of the Lynchburg City Code, Title 58.1 of the Code of Virginia and Article X of the Virginia Constitution, and it keeps an alphabetical ownership tax roll for each July 1 to June 30 period.

Every parcel is reassessed every two years, so a Lynchburg owner can see a value change without making any improvement. Transfers and building permits are handled all year, so a new deck or a sale can shift a record between reassessments. The office also prepares special appraisal estimates for budgeting and rental studies from time to time, and those are separate from your tax bill.

Get the next installment date from the Treasurer and the appeal window from the Assessor.

Start with the Assessor, whose office page has an Appeals section. Virginia also gives a correction route in Va. Code 58.1-3980 for errors made by the assessing official or caused by a factual mistake in a general reassessment.

  • The correction request goes to the official who made the assessment.
  • Time limit: three years counted from the final day of the tax year, or one year from the assessment date if that ends later.
  • For real estate the statute applies only when the error is the assessor's or a factual error made during reassessment.
  • A disagreement about value alone follows the city's own review process, which the Assessor can explain.

Keep photos, repair bids and comparable sales ready, since any appeal rests on evidence.

A real estate tax lien in Virginia comes before all other liens, which is why the closing agent takes delinquent tax from the seller's proceeds. Va. Code 58.1-3340 requires the purchaser or foreclosure trustee to apply sale proceeds to assessed taxes and levies, penalties and interest included.

Once paid, the treasurer releases the lien, and the current year's share is prorated under your contract. Under Va. Code 58.1-802 the seller also pays a grantor's tax of 50 cents per $500 of consideration unless buyer and seller agree otherwise, and the clerk of court collects it at recording.

Thinking about a quick sale? Get the exact payoff from the Treasurer, and have the title company confirm any lien before you sign.

sections.h2: Why your value can change between cycles
sections.html:
Cycles are not the whole story. A sale that goes through, or a building permit that is finished, can prompt the office to update the record at any time. If you built a deck last spring and the record changed afterward, that is the process working as designed rather than a mistake. A change you did not cause is different. Check the ParcelViewer record for square footage, bedroom and bath counts and lot size, and hold it up against the house you really own. A data mistake is the simplest kind to fix.

Winter and summer both matter to inspectors. Average temperatures run from 35.9 degrees F in January to 76.0 degrees F in July, with about 27.4 days a year at 90 degrees or higher and about 11.6 inches of snow a season, so roof and heating condition deserve documentation before a showing.

Remember that exempt parcels, about 1,645 of them, are carved out of the roll. If your parcel has an exemption or program status, ask the Assessor what a sale does to it.

sections.h2: A short checklist before you list
sections.html:
1. Look up your parcel on ParcelViewer and confirm the details are right.
  2. Phone the Treasurer at the city for the next installment date and any balance.
  3. Call the Assessor at 434-455-3830 about the appeal window if the value looks high.
  4. Collect photos, repair bids and comparable sales in one folder.
  5. Ask the title company to start a lien search early, so nothing surprises you near closing.

That order puts the cheap questions first. A phone call to the Treasurer costs nothing and tells you more about your closing costs than any estimate.

The city's tax period runs July 1 to June 30, which means a house sold mid-year has a tax year that is only partly used. Your contract decides how the months are divided, and the settlement agent turns that into a line on your statement. Ask to see the dates used. When the first installment is already paid, the buyer typically repays you for the rest of the year after closing. If an installment is still open, the agent will usually deduct your share from your proceeds and pay the Treasurer.

The deed's grantor tax is its own item, and the seller pays it unless both sides agree to something else. Because the clerk collects it at recording, you will see it as a charge at the table rather than on a city bill.

With no lender involved, a cash sale has few steps: ask for an offer, let the buyer look at the house as is, then a title company takes care of the deed, pays off the tax and records the deed with the circuit court clerk. Beforehand, pull together your latest tax bill, any Assessor notice and the names on the deed. Where the owner has died, say so early, since a personal representative's authority must be documented before anyone can sign a deed.

Set on the James River in the Blue Ridge foothills, Lynchburg is an independent city. The population was 79,009 in 2020 and is estimated at 81,347 for 2025. Its nickname, the City of Seven Hills, describes terrain that shapes lot lines, driveways and retaining walls. The river that built the town also flooded it, with floods in 1842, 1847, 1870 and 1877, so a house near the water deserves a closer look at drainage than one on a ridge.

The city has ten recognized historic districts, four of them in the downtown residential area. Court House Hill-Downtown, Daniel's Hill, Diamond Hill, Federal Hill, Garland Hill and Rivermont are among them. Before selling or renovating inside a district, ask city planning staff which review applies. Buyers rely on U.S. routes, because no Interstate reaches Lynchburg, the state's largest city without one.

faqs.q: What is the Lynchburg property tax rate?
faqs.a: The City Assessor's page lists $0.84 per $100 of assessed value for 2025 to 2026. City Council sets the rate, so confirm it for the current year.

faqs.q: How often does Lynchburg reassess property?
faqs.a: All parcels are reassessed every two years. Transfers and building permits are processed throughout the year.

faqs.q: Where is the Lynchburg City Assessor's office?
faqs.a: It is at 900 Church Street, Lynchburg, VA 24504, phone 434-455-3830, open Monday through Friday from 8:30 am to 5 pm.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Lynchburg house with property tax owed?
faqs.a: Yes. The tax lien is paid from the sale proceeds at closing, and the treasurer releases it. Get a payoff figure first so the title company can plan for it.

faqs.q: Where do I find Lynchburg due dates and appeal deadlines?
faqs.a: Call the City Treasurer for due dates and the City Assessor for appeal deadlines.
